articles.title: Clinical and Molecular Genetic Testing Risk Stratification for Pediatric Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma Therapy.
articles.abstract:
Children and young adolescents with papillary thyroid cancer (CAYA-PTC) have high recurrence rates. Current guidelines advocate intensive treatment, yet existing risk stratification systems lack integration of genomic characteristics and provide limited precision in guiding surgical extent and postoperative radioactive iodine (RAI).

This retrospective, multicenter study analyzed 435 CAYA-PTC patients (ages 2-18 years) treated between 2006 and 2024. A clinicogenomic nomogram for disease-free survival (DFS) was developed using clinical data, postoperative pathology, and molecular testing of surgical tissue. Patients were stratified according to the nomogram score. Model performance was internally compared with the American Thyroid Association (ATA) pediatric risk system. Treatment associations were assessed by surgical extent (total thyroidectomy vs lobectomy) and receipt of postoperative RAI therapy within each risk stratification.

Five variables were independent predictors of worse DFS: age ≤15 years, tumor size >4 cm, lateral neck node involvement (N1b), coexisting Hashimoto thyroiditis, and RET/NTRK fusions (all P <.05). The nomogram stratified patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups with 7-year DFS rates of 92.4%, 83.1%, and 56.4% (P <.001). In internal comparison, nomogram-based risk stratification had higher concordance index (0.721 vs 0.656) and 3-year AUC (0.748 vs 0.651) values than ATA stratification (both P <.05). Total thyroidectomy was associated with better DFS in intermediate- and high-risk patients but not low-risk patients. Higher DFS with postoperative RAI was observed in the high-risk group (P =.028).

Using retrospective clinicogenomic features, our stratification suggests a risk-adapted framework for CAYA-PTC. However, non-significant differences, especially in small subgroups, do not establish treatment equivalence or confirm the safety of de-escalation. These findings represent associations that require future external validation.
articles.journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism
articles.clinical_bottom_line: However, non-significant differences, especially in small subgroups, do not establish treatment equivalence or confirm the safety of de-escalation. These findings represent associations that require future external validation.

articles.title: Serum FGF-21 levels and stature in children and adolescents with celiac disease on a gluten-free diet.
articles.abstract:
To evaluate stature in patients with celiac disease (CD) adherent to a gluten-free diet (GFD), determine the prevalence of growth hormone deficiency (GHD), and assess the associations between stature and serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 3 (IGFBP-3), and FGF 21 levels.

In this prospective cross-sectional study, 141 pediatric patients with CD (79 females) who had adhered to a GFD for at least 2 years were included. Anthropometric and clinical data were obtained from medical records. Serum IGF-1, IGFBP-3, and FGF21 levels were measured in fasting samples. Growth hormone stimulation tests (L-dopa and clonidine) were performed in patients with a height >1.5 SDS below target height (TH).

Twelve patients (8.5 %) had persistent short stature despite long-term adherence to a GFD. Growth hormone deficiency was diagnosed in three patients (2.1 % of the entire cohort; 25 % of patients with persistent short stature). Patients with persistent short stature without GHD had significantly lower serum IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 standard deviation scores than those with normal stature, whereas serum FGF21 concentrations did not differ significantly between the groups. Serum FGF21 concentrations were not significantly correlated with height SDS, IGF-1, IGFBP-3, or other anthropometric variables.

Persistent short stature may occur despite long-term adherence to a GFD in a small proportion of children and adolescents with CD. GHD was identified in 2.1 % of patients, emphasizing the importance of growth monitoring. Lower IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 SDS in patients with persistent short stature without GHD suggest alterations within the GH-IGF axis. Serum FGF21 concentrations were not associated with stature, suggesting that persistent growth impairment in treated CD is likely multifactorial and is not explained by circulating FGF21 alone.
articles.journal: Journal of pediatric endocrinology & metabolism : JPEM
articles.clinical_bottom_line: Lower IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 SDS in patients with persistent short stature without GHD suggest alterations within the GH-IGF axis. Serum FGF21 concentrations were not associated with stature, suggesting that persistent growth impairment in treated CD is likely multifactorial and is not explained by circulating FGF21 alone.

articles.title: Somatrogon versus somatropin in children with growth hormone deficiency: a real-world matched-cohort study.
articles.abstract:
Somatrogon is a once-weekly growth hormone (GH) analog approved for GH deficiency (GHD), but real-world head-to-head data are limited. Using a matched-cohort design with a protocol-defined IGF-1 sampling time, we compared first-year growth outcomes and safety of somatrogon and daily somatropin in children with GHD.

We conducted a retrospective matched-cohort study in 30 children with GHD (15 per group) at a single center. Groups were matched by age (±1 year), sex, and pubertal stage. Annual height velocity (AHV), height standard deviation score (SDS) gain, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) SDS, insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3 (IGFBP-3), bone age advancement, and metabolic parameters were assessed at 12 months.

AHV was similar in both groups (8.96±1.67 vs 8.84±1.57 cm/year; p=0.841). Height SDS gain did not differ (0.60±0.36 vs 0.53±0.33; p=0.569). IGF-1 SDS was numerically higher in the somatrogon group (+0.59 vs -0.14; p=0.132) but remained within safe limits in all patients. Bone age advancement, glucose, and insulin levels were similar between groups. No adverse events or injection-site reactions were documented during follow-up.

In this matched cohort, no significant differences in growth or safety outcomes were observed between somatrogon and somatropin at one year. Somatrogon appears to be a reasonable alternative to daily GH therapy in children with GHD.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: In this matched cohort, no significant differences in growth or safety outcomes were observed between somatrogon and somatropin at one year. Somatrogon appears to be a reasonable alternative to daily GH therapy in children with GHD.
articles.impact_rationale: Observational/Cohort on Growth. Background reading for clinical awareness.

articles.title: Cortisol Cutoffs for Adrenal Insufficiency Using Elecsys II: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract:
Adrenal insufficiency (AI) is associated with increased risk of morbidity and mortality if improperly managed. Adrenocorticotrophin (ACTH) stimulation testing is the most widely used AI diagnostic test. Historically, a serum cortisol threshold of 500 nmol/L (18.1 µg/dL), derived using polyclonal assays, was widely used. Improved monoclonal immunoassays show reduced cross-reactivity and lower cortisol values, but no universally accepted ACTH-stimulated cortisol threshold exists. Suggestions ranging between 348 and 485 nmol/L [12.6-17.6 µg/dL] reflect methodology and cohort differences. Our objective was to systematically review the literature and recommend a revised cortisol threshold.

We searched MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English language studies published between January 2016 and 19 September 2023 (PROSPERO CRD42023479405). Eligible studies reported original data, used the Roche Elecsys II assay, and recommended a cortisol threshold. Quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework, and risk of bias with the ArRoWS questionnaire. Multiple suggested thresholds based on ROC, sensitivity/specificity, or regression analysis were identified.

Six studies involving 1799 samples from 430 adult and paediatric patients were included. A serum cortisol cutoff of 405 nmol/L (14.7 µg/dL) was defined based on synthesis, sensitivity analysis, and a conservative approach to reduce false‑negatives.

We affirm recommendations to lower the cortisol threshold for AI when using monoclonal assays. A peak threshold of 405 nmol/L (14.7 µg/dL) is suggested for a standard-dose ACTH test on the Elecsys II assay for diagnosis of AI, acknowledging limitations related to the small number and GRADE quality of included studies.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: We affirm recommendations to lower the cortisol threshold for AI when using monoclonal assays. A peak threshold of 405 nmol/L (14.7 µg/dL) is suggested for a standard-dose ACTH test on the Elecsys II assay for diagnosis of AI, acknowledging limitations related to the small number and GRADE quality of included studies.
articles.impact_rationale: Systematic review of Adrenal evidence. Level I synthesis; strongest available summary short of a guideline.

articles.title: Association of HbA1c with Time in Range, Time in Tight Range, Empirically Derived Continuous Glucose Monitoring Glucose Ranges, and Mean Glucose.
articles.abstract:
To evaluate how continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) glucose thresholds, sampling duration, and statistical modeling influence associations between CGM-derived range metrics and HbA1c, and to compare empirically derived glucose ranges with time in range (TIR) and time in tight range (TITR).

Out of 8160 HbA1c-matched CGM datasets from 1584 adults, CGM data from the 14, 30, and 90 days preceding each HbA1c measurement were evaluated. Associations between HbA1c and 7790 CGM glucose ranges were assessed across varying lower and upper glucose thresholds. Linear and log-linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and race with participant-level random intercepts were compared using root mean square error and marginal. Participant-level derivation (80%) and validation (20%) cohorts were used for cross-validated threshold selection and discrimination analyses for HbA1c ≤7.0%.

Ninety-day CGM sampling showed the strongest associations with HbA1c. Log-linear models frequently provided comparable or improved fit, particularly for glucose ranges with upper thresholds below 180 mg/dL. Stronger HbA1c associations clustered around upper glucose thresholds of 155-175 mg/dL. In validation analyses, empirically derived ranges demonstrated strong discrimination of HbA1c ≤7.0% (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.909-0.915), compared with 0.903 for TIR and 0.905 for TITR, although absolute differences were small. Mean glucose demonstrated the strongest explanatory performance for continuous HbA1c (marginal= 0.74) and similarly strong discrimination (AUC 0.913).

CGM-HbA1c relationships are influenced by glucose range, sampling duration, and statistical modeling. Our findings reinforce TIR and TITR as robust CGM metrics with strong associations with HbA1c, while also showing that selected empirically derived glucose ranges can provide modestly stronger statistical alignment. These results support the continued use of TIR and TITR while highlighting how glucose range definition may refine interpretation of CGM-based endpoints in future research.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: Our findings reinforce TIR and TITR as robust CGM metrics with strong associations with HbA1c, while also showing that selected empirically derived glucose ranges can provide modestly stronger statistical alignment. These results support the continued use of TIR and TITR while highlighting how glucose range definition may refine interpretation of CGM-based endpoints in future research.

articles.title: Permanent congenital hypothyroidism withp.Leu187Pro: clinical follow-up data and epigenetic insights.
articles.abstract:
variants have recently been identified as a novel cause of congenital hypothyroidism (CH), but the clinical spectrum remains incompletely defined. Longitudinal data on methylation dynamics at cg12054698, an open-sea CpG site within the5' untranslated region (5' UTR), and normative methylation levels in euthyroid controls are lacking.

We identified three unrelated CH probands carrying the heterozygousp.Leu187Pro variant by trio whole-exome sequencing and systematically screened 61 known CH-related genes. Clinical phenotypes and longitudinal outcomes data were collected. For epigenetic analysis, cg12054698 methylation was quantified by pyrosequencing in the three probands, their carrier parents, 30 age-stratified euthyroid controls (newborns, toddlers, and adults), 10 CH patients withoutvariants, and paired longitudinal samples from two probands.

All three probands presented with moderate-to-severe CH at neonatal diagnosis. Thyroid ultrasonography revealed heterogeneous phenotypes, including a normalgland, thyroid agenesis, and a normal-sized gland with diffuse hypoechogenicity. All three cases were confirmed as permanent CH. In euthyroid controls, cg12054698 methylation was significantly higher in newborns than in toddlers and adults (p<0.001). Neonatal methylation levels did not differ significantly among probands withvariants, CH patients withoutvariants, and euthyroid controls (p=0.260).

In this cohort,-associated CH was permanent and showed a marked phenotypic heterogeneity. cg12054698 was hypermethylated during the neonatal period across study groups, supporting a developmentally regulated, stage-specific epigenetic pattern rather than a disease-specific pathogenic "second hit."

articles.clinical_bottom_line: In this cohort,-associated CH was permanent and showed a marked phenotypic heterogeneity. cg12054698 was hypermethylated during the neonatal period across study groups, supporting a developmentally regulated, stage-specific epigenetic pattern rather than a disease-specific pathogenic "second hit."

articles.title: Weight Maintenance Following Discontinuation of Semaglutide in an Adolescent with Antipsychotic-Associated Weight Gain: A Case Report.
articles.abstract:
Antipsychotic-induced weight gain (AIWG) presents a significant clinical challenge in pediatric psychiatry, often leading to Class II or III obesity and metabolic comorbidities. While treatment with metformin is the current standard of care, its efficacy is often modest. Preclinical and translational data suggest that, by targeting the underlying cause of AIWG, GLP-1Ras may help restore satiety signaling that is disrupted in patients taking antipsychotics.

We describe an adolescent who experienced profound weight gain following aripiprazole treatment which was successfully managed with semaglutide. Notably, after achieving therapeutic goals of normalization of body mass index (BMI) and hemoglobin A1c, the patient was able to discontinue semaglutide while maintaining her weight loss and normalization of hemoglobin A1c over six months of follow-up.

This single case raises the hypothesis that GLP-1RAs could serve as a temporary "bridge therapy" to counteract iatrogenic metabolic insults; given the confounding factors discussed below, this observation is hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in larger, prospective studies before broader clinical application.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: Notably, after achieving therapeutic goals of normalization of body mass index (BMI) and hemoglobin A1c, the patient was able to discontinue semaglutide while maintaining her weight loss and normalization of hemoglobin A1c over six months of follow-up. This single case raises the hypothesis that GLP-1RAs could serve as a temporary "bridge therapy" to counteract iatrogenic metabolic insults; given the confounding factors discussed below, this observation is hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in larger, prospective studies before broader clinical application.

articles.title: Thyroid Abnormalities in a Prospective Longitudinal Cohort of Pediatric Patients following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
articles.abstract: Introduction Thyroid dysfunction has been reported in adults and children following COVID-19. We evaluated thyroid function in children following SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to uninfected controls over at least one year of follow up. Methods Thyroid function tests (TSH, Free T4) were analyzed in pediatric participants enrolled in the Pediatric SARS CoV-2 Long Term Outcome Study (PECOS), a diverse, prospective, longitudinal, multicenter cohort study. Assessments were conducted at baseline, and at follow-up visits for both infected and uninfected cohorts. Results Among 505 participants with non-missing data at baseline and 12-months, no significant differences were noted in proportion of TSH or Free T4 abnormalities among the infected vs. uninfected participants. Among infected participants 5% (25/464) developed subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH and normal free T4) following recovery from SARS-CoV-2 infection, compared with 4.9% (2/41), a similar proportion in the uninfected group (p=1). Within the infected subgroup during 36-month follow up, three were treated with levothyroxine for persistent TSH elevation or goiter and 2/3 had positive thyroid antibodies consistent with autoimmune thyroid disease. Neither the number of SARS-CoV-2 reinfections nor number of COVID-19 vaccination status predicted the occurrence of TSH abnormalities. Conclusion Children infected with COVID-19 did not have increased thyroid dysfunction compared to uninfected controls during 12 months of follow up. A small proportion (5%) developed mild subclinical hypothyroidism that was transient in both groups, and only 3 infected participants (with TSH>10mcIU/mL or thyromegaly) needed levothyroxine replacement after 36-month follow up in this subgroup. Risk of thyroid autoimmunity compared to the uninfected population needs further study.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: A small proportion (5%) developed mild subclinical hypothyroidism that was transient in both groups, and only 3 infected participants (with TSH>10mcIU/mL or thyromegaly) needed levothyroxine replacement after 36-month follow up in this subgroup. Risk of thyroid autoimmunity compared to the uninfected population needs further study.
articles.impact_rationale: Observational study on Thyroid. Cohort size n = 505. Clinically informative but limited by non-randomized design.

articles.title: Pediatric Inpatient Continuous Glucose Monitoring: Development and Implementation of a Hospital Policy for Accuracy-Validated Insulin Dosing.
articles.abstract:
We assessed the safety, clinical accuracy, glycemic outcomes, user outcomes, and implementation of a pediatric hospital-wide continuous glucose monitor (CGM) policy.

We used the Model for Improvement to develop a pediatric hospital policy supporting CGM-based insulin dosing with accuracy validation using capillary finger-stick blood glucose (FSBG) and then retrospectively evaluated the program's clinical effectiveness and implementation outcomes with the Simplified Implementation Logic Model to connect contextual determinants, support strategies, and outcomes.

From September 2024 to October 2025, 60 people with diabetes used the CGM policy in 93 hospital encounters, including 46.7% (28/60) people with type 1 diabetes and 38.7% (36/93) encounters with automated insulin delivery use. The most used CGMs were Dexcom G7 (49.5%) and Abbott Libre 3 or 3 Plus (31.2%). Accuracy validation using the %20/20 criteria was successful in 81.5% of attempts, and the mean absolute relative difference was 12.6%, with 1207 paired CGM and reference FSBG values. Nurses responded appropriately after 97.8% (218/223) of failed CGM validation attempts. CGM time in range (70-180 mg/dL) was 54.8%, and time in level 2 hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL) was 0.8% for the 58 out of 93 encounters with complete CGM data downloads. Nurses preferred using CGM with policy support instead of FSBG for insulin dosing (adjusted= 0.046). Factors contributing to nursing preference included ease of use, system integration, and the ability to learn the system quickly.

We translated an inpatient CGM policy from an adult to pediatric hospital setting, supporting high levels of protocol adherence, clinical accuracy, safety, and improved experiences for clinicians. Program evaluation informs connections between contextual determinants, support strategies, and outcomes of implementing a hospital CGM program. These data offer a roadmap for implementing pediatric hospital CGM at other centers.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: Program evaluation informs connections between contextual determinants, support strategies, and outcomes of implementing a hospital CGM program. These data offer a roadmap for implementing pediatric hospital CGM at other centers.

articles.title: Mild TSH elevation is independently associated with height in children.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate whether mildly elevated thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) (<10 mIU/L) is associated with height in children independently of the growth hormone-insulin-like growth factor 1 (GH-IGF-1) axis, and to assess sex differences.
METHODS: This retrospective cross-sectional study included 2,447 children aged 2-10 years presenting for slow growth evaluation (2022-2024). Multivariable linear regression was used with adjustment for age, sex, and IGF-1 SDS; restricted cubic splines (RCS) were used to assess the dose-response relationship. Sex-stratified and sensitivity analyses were performed.
RESULTS: Mildly elevated TSH was present in 96 (3.92 %) children. Overall, TSH was inversely associated with height SDS (β=-0.03, p<0.001) independently of IGF-1; RCS confirmed linearity. The association was significant in boys (β=-0.03, p=0.002) and borderline in girls. Boys with elevated TSH had lower height SDS (β=-0.18, p=0.025). Sensitivity analyses: the association persisted after excluding low IGF-1 (β=-0.02, p=0.004) but not in children with short stature (height SDS ≤-2).
CONCLUSIONS: Mildly elevated TSH is independently associated with reduced height in children aged 2-10 years, independent of IGF-1. The association was significant in boys and borderline in girls, with no significant interaction. The absence of bone age and parental height data is a major limitation. These findings support growth monitoring rather than routine levothyroxine therapy.
articles.journal: Journal of pediatric endocrinology & metabolism : JPEM
articles.clinical_bottom_line: Mildly elevated TSH is independently associated with reduced height in children aged 2-10 years, independent of IGF-1. The association was significant in boys and borderline in girls, with no significant interaction.

articles.title: Laboratory-based case finding using phosphate and alkaline phosphatase to identify genetic and nutritional rickets in children.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Hypophosphatemic rickets is a rare disease characterized by renal phosphate loss, leading to chronic hypophosphatemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and skeletal symptoms that may remain unnoticed until advanced stages. Early diagnosis is essential because effective treatment is available to reduce complications.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate a laboratory-based case-finding strategy for identifying oligosymptomatic patients with hypophosphatemic rickets using phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase results in a pediatric population.
METHODS: A descriptive observational study was conducted in patients under 18 years of age at a tertiary care hospital between June 2021 and July 2025. Of 47,127 phosphorus or alkaline phosphatase measurements requested, 45,923 measurements corresponding to 28,045 tests from 12,513 patients were analyzed after exclusions. Test showing hypophosphatemia and/or elevated alkaline phosphatase were identified, and X-rays and clinical data were reviewed for classification.
RESULTS: A total of 22,860 phosphorus measurements and 23,063 alkaline phosphatase measurements were analyzed, with both parameters available in 17,878 laboratory tests. Hypophosphatemia was observed in 2,281 phosphorus measurements (9.98%), and elevated alkaline phosphatase in 3,301 measurements (14.3%). Fifty-five laboratory tests (0.31%) from 37 patients simultaneously met the criteria for hypophosphatemia (<-2 SD) and elevated alkaline phosphatase (>+2 SD); 56.8% were male, with a mean age of 6.5 ± 6.0 years. Following clinical review, 15 patients (40.5%) were classified as having a bone mineral metabolism disorder, including 10 with osteopenia of prematurity, three with nutritional rickets, one with a pathogenic variant in PHEX, and one with osteoporosis in the context of ReNU syndrome; 10 patients (27.0%) were classified in the acute/critical illness group and 12 (32.4%) in the other category. Radiographs were available in 30 patients, with findings consistent with rickets in three (10%). One previously unrecognized case of mild nutritional rickets was identified.
CONCLUSIONS: Laboratory-based case finding using phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase may help identify pediatric bone metabolism disorders, including forms of rickets. Combined hypophosphatemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase may be useful for guiding etiological investigation. This approach may complement clinical evaluation and facilitate earlier diagnosis. Early identification is clinically relevant because treatments can modify disease course and reduce long-term complications in children with confirmed forms of rickets, when appropriate.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: Laboratory-based case finding using phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase may help identify pediatric bone metabolism disorders, including forms of rickets. Combined hypophosphatemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase may be useful for guiding etiological investigation.

articles.title: Evaluating the implementation of the Diabetes Body Project in a clinical cohort of Australian adolescents with type 1 diabetes.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1D) are at increased risk of disordered eating behaviors (DEB) and eating disorders (ED) compared to their peers without T1D, contributing to increased diabetes-related complications, and elevated mortality risk. Despite this, there is a lack of targeted ED prevention interventions specifically designed for adolescents with T1D, within routine clinical care. The Diabetes Body Project (DBP) has demonstrated promising feasibility, acceptability, and reduction of DEB in young adults; however, its application in younger adolescents and real-world clinical settings has not been tested.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to extend previous DBP research by evaluating its implementation within a real-world Australian clinical service. The study will assess feasibility and acceptability and explore preliminary efficacy in relation to DEB and glycaemic control in an exclusively adolescent population, including a novel parent/caregiver component.
METHODS: This protocol describes a pilot study that will recruit 24 female adolescents with T1D from the John Hunter Children's Hospital (JHCH) Diabetes Service in New South Wales, Australia, along with up to 24 parents/caregivers. Adolescents will participate in a 6-week virtually delivered manualised cognitive dissonance based DBP program, delivered in a group format across four cohorts of 6 adolescents. In addition, two group sessions will be developed and delivered virtually to parents/caregivers for each cohort. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, post-intervention and at 3 and 6 months follow up. Feasibility will be evaluated through recruitment, retention, attendance, between-session activity completion and parent/caregiver uptake. Acceptability will be assessed via participant and caregiver satisfaction surveys. Preliminary efficacy will be explored through changes in disordered eating behaviors (Diabetes Eating Problem Survey-Revised), body appreciation (BAS-2), diabetes distress (PAID-T), and glycaemic outcomes.
DISCUSSION: This study will evaluate the implementation of an adapted DBP intervention for adolescents with T1D within a real-world clinical service. By incorporating a novel parent/caregiver component and targeting the adolescent population, the study addresses key gaps in current literature. Findings may inform the design of future larger-scale trials and support the integration of ED prevention strategies into routine pediatric diabetes care.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: By incorporating a novel parent/caregiver component and targeting the adolescent population, the study addresses key gaps in current literature. Findings may inform the design of future larger-scale trials and support the integration of ED prevention strategies into routine pediatric diabetes care.

articles.title: When diabetic ketoacidosis becomes a neurological emergency: cerebral edema in a child with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus - a case report and narrative review.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D), potentially leading to severe outcomes, including cerebral edema (CE). The case describes an eight-year-old child with previously undiagnosed T1D complicated by DKA, and subsequent development of CE. It is followed by a short literature review including other pediatric cases of clinically overt CE.
CASE PRESENTATION: A boy was admitted to the outpatient clinic with a several-day history of vomiting, abdominal pain and headache, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of gastrointestinal infection. The following day, the patient's condition deteriorated. Despite a positive family history of T1D (the patient's father), his blood glucose level was measured for the first time by the emergency medical service (25.6 mmol/L (460 mg/dL)). Further evaluation revealed DKA secondary to previously undiagnosed T1D. On admission, the boy was in severe general condition. Severe DKA was confirmed (pH 6.88), and appropriate treatment was implemented, resulting in temporary clinical stabilization. However, on the second day of hospitalization, the patient's condition deteriorated again. He was somnolent, with fluctuating consciousness and nuchal rigidity. An increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) was suspected. Optic nerve ultrasonography revealed increased optic nerve sheath diameters, also suggestive of raised ICP. Anti-edema therapy with mannitol was initiated based on clinical suspicion, resulting in clinical improvement. Dexamethasone and furosemide were administered as adjunctive therapy. Subsequent CT findings supported the diagnosis of CE. The patient was discharged after 10 days in good general condition.
CONCLUSIONS: DKA can be a diagnostic challenge for clinicians due to its nonspecific symptoms. Early signs suggesting this condition should not be underestimated, and bedside blood glucose should be measured early in children presenting with unexplained vomiting, weight loss, tachypnea, dehydration or altered consciousness. Close monitoring for complications is critical during treatment, especially for CE, one of the most serious and potentially life-threatening consequences of DKA.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: DKA can be a diagnostic challenge for clinicians due to its nonspecific symptoms. Early signs suggesting this condition should not be underestimated, and bedside blood glucose should be measured early in children presenting with unexplained vomiting, weight loss, tachypnea, dehydration or altered consciousness.

articles.title: Management of pregnancy in patients with Graves' disease secondary to alemtuzumab: a case series and literature review.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Alemtuzumab treatment for multiple sclerosis frequently induces Graves' disease (GD), characterized by common coexistence of stimulating and blocking anti-thyrotropin receptor autoantibodies (TRAb), causing fluctuations of thyroid function. Alemtuzumab-induced TRAb-positive hypothyroidism is also common. These conditions are challenging to manage during pregnancy, considering the imperative necessity to maintain euthyroidism to minimize risks for both pregnancy and fetal/neonatal outcomes.
METHODS: We reviewed the clinical course and therapeutic management of four pregnant women affected with alemtuzumab-induced GD or TRAb-positive hypothyroidism followed at our Institution, and seven additional cases published in literature.
RESULTS: At our institution two patients with alemtuzumab-induced GD (one diagnosed before pregnancy, the other during the third trimester) showed a good control of thyroid function on anti-thyroid drugs (ATD). Two women had alemtuzumab-induced TRAb positive hypothyroidism; during pregnancy thyroid function was partially controlled with levothyroxine (LT4) alone in one case, and fully controlled with block and replace (ATD and LT4) in the other case. No pregnancy or fetal/neonatal negative outcomes were observed, except for preterm delivery of a healthy baby in Case 3, due to emergency cesarean section for pre-eclampsia progressing to HELLP syndrome. The literature search showed seven additional cases of pregnant women with alemtuzumab-induced GD (N = 5) or TRAb-positive hypothyroidism (N = 2), mainly diagnosed during gestation, especially in the first trimester. Six newborns developed transient thyroid dysfunction, often requiring treatment and later resolved.
CONCLUSION: The clinical management of alemtuzumab-induced thyroid dysfunction during pregnancy is challenged by frequent difficult maternal biochemical thyroid control and TRAb-mediated fetal/neonatal thyroid dysfunction. These patients need to be managed in a specialist setting, with close monitoring of maternal thyroid function and fetal/neonatal parameters, especially in cases with high TRAb titers.
articles.clinical_bottom_line: The clinical management of alemtuzumab-induced thyroid dysfunction during pregnancy is challenged by frequent difficult maternal biochemical thyroid control and TRAb-mediated fetal/neonatal thyroid dysfunction. These patients need to be managed in a specialist setting, with close monitoring of maternal thyroid function and fetal/neonatal parameters, especially in cases with high TRAb titers.
